raw_case_text: A 50-year-old married female from Chitwan District presented with fever for 9 days which was high grade, intermittent, measuring up to 104 degrees Fahrenheit and associated with chills, rigors, and sweating. Also she gave history of body ache, weakness, nausea, vomiting, headache, and yellowish discoloration of eyes. She noticed small rash over her right shoulder a few days after first episode of fever which gradually took the shape of cigarette burn eschar. She gave history of regular visit to jungle for cutting wood and grazing cattle. With these symptoms she first visited OPD on 6th day of illness where few tests were run; follow-up was done on 7th day where diagnosis of dengue was made and admitted for one day at local hospital where she received injection ceftriaxone and tablet azithromycin. The investigations revealed low platelets count for which two-pint PRP were transfused. With persistent symptoms and low platelets count, she was referred to our centre the next day. At presentation, she was well oriented to time, place, and person. Her blood pressure was 100/60 mm of Hg, pulse rate was 98 beats per minute, temperature was 100 F, and respiratory rate was 22 per minute. On general physical examination she was icteric with palpable axillary lymph nodes bilaterally and pitting edema was present. Eschar was visible on right deltoid with necrotic centre forming scab and erythematous periphery (Figure 1). Also similar eschar was found on Rt waist (Figure 2). There was hepatosplenomegaly with liver span of 16 cm and spleen was palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin. Occasional crackles were heard in right infra-axillary and inframammary region. Apart from these the other systemic examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory investigations revealed leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia. Her LFTs were deranged with raised total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, SGOT, SGPT, ALP, and LDH. Her PT was prolonged. Sodium and potassium were below normal. Values of all these parameters are listed in Table 1. The peripheral blood smear did not show malarial parasite. Serology was nonreactive for HIV, HBS Ag, and HCV. USG showed hepatomegaly with fatty liver grade II and right pleural effusion. CXR showed right pleural effusion. ECG was normal. With these findings empirical treatment was started with iv ceftriaxone and tablet doxycycline. Further reports showed that IgM/IgG antibody for Leptospira was negative, IgM/IgG antibody for dengue was positive (method: immunochromatography), and Widal agglutination test for Salmonella typhi and S. paratyphi was negative. Intravenous fluid and electrolytes were supplemented while oral doxycycline was continued. Report for scrub typhus was awaited. The test result was obtained on 5th day of admission from National Public Health Laboratory, Teku. Scrub typhus was positive (method: ELISA). She was discharged on 7th day of admission and advised for follow-up in a week. But the patient was followed up only after two weeks at local hospital in her hometown where lab investigations were carried out and were normal. She has been doing well since then and this was confirmed by telephone conversation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old female presenting with high-grade fever for 9 days, chills, rigors, sweating, headache, vomiting, jaundice, and two eschars.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 50-year-old female presented with a 9-day history of high-grade intermittent fever (up to 104 F) with chills, rigors, and sweating, alongside body aches, weakness, headache, nausea, vomiting, and scleral icterus. A few days after fever onset, she noted a skin lesion on her right shoulder that enlarged into a cigarette-burn eschar, and another lesion on her right waist. She was seen at a local clinic on day 6 and hospital on day 7 where she received IV ceftriaxone, oral azithromycin, and 2 pints of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) for thrombocytopenia before transfer due to persistent fever and cytopenias.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological history: Regular visits to the jungle for cutting wood and grazing cattle in Chitwan District. Prior medical history otherwise unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, generalized body aches, weakness, nausea, vomiting, headache, jaundice, and skin lesions. Negative for chest pain or cough. Prior medications: IV ceftriaxone, oral azithromycin, and 2 units PRP at local hospital. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 100 F, blood pressure: 100/60 mmHg, pulse rate: 98 beats/min, respiratory rate: 22 breaths/min. Alert and oriented x3. Icteric. Bilateral palpable axillary lymphadenopathy and peripheral pitting edema present. Skin: Cigarette-burn eschar with necrotic center, black scab, and erythematous periphery on right deltoid and right waist. Abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly (liver span 16 cm; spleen palpable 2 cm below left costal margin). Respiratory: Occasional crackles in right infra-axillary and inframammary regions.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia. LFTs: Raised total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, SGOT, SGPT, ALP, and LDH. Coagulation: Prolonged PT. Electrolytes: Hyponatremia and hypokalemia. Peripheral blood smear: Negative for malaria parasites. Serology: Nonreactive for HIV, HBsAg, HCV, Leptospira (IgM/IgG), and Widal test (Salmonella typhi/paratyphi negative). Chest X-ray: Right pleural effusion. Abdominal ultrasound: Hepatomegaly with grade II fatty liver and right pleural effusion. ECG: Normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute co-infection of Dengue fever and Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) with hepatosplenomegaly, transaminitis, jaundice, and right pleural effusion. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus IgM and IgG serology (immunochromatography) and positive Scrub typhus ELISA (confirmed by National Public Health Laboratory, Teku); negative malaria smears and Leptospira/Widal/viral hepatitis serology.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with IV ceftriaxone, oral doxycycline, IV fluid and electrolyte repletion. Discharged on day 7 of admission in improved condition; normal laboratory values at 2-week follow-up at local hospital and doing well.
